newsitem.title: CHINA: Unpaid fees trouble China's venture leasing firms.
newsitem.headline: Unpaid fees trouble China's venture leasing firms.

text.p: China's joint venture financial leasing firms, set up in the 1980s to finance the state sector, are troubled by mounting unpaid fees but say continued profits mean they will remain in the market.
"Our unpaid fees are approaching $100 million," said an official of the Beijing-based China Orient Leasing Co, the first Sino-foreign joint venture leasing firm to be set up in China.
"We made a loss last year," he said, without giving further details.

The major shareholder in China Orient Leasing, set up in 1981, is Japan's Orix Corp with a 50 percent stake. The China International Trust and Investment Corp holds 20 percent and Beijing Mechanical and Electrical Equipment Co the rest.
Many joint venture leasing firms have been hit by rising unpaid fees from state firms, most of which entered into leasing agreements in the 1980s, the official said.
Under most of the contracts, leasing firms purchased advanced foreign equipment and leased it to cash-strapped state firms, the official said.

China's economic reforms have cut many government ties with state enterprises and turned them loose in the marketplace, he said. In addition, reforms have weakened the financial strength of local governments who had been the guarantors.
"Local governments can no longer perform their duty as guarantors," the official said.
Many state firms have failed to perform as well as expected because of difficulties in adapting to the market.
"Currently, the economic efficiency of state firms is not good," he said. "Many are having repayment difficulties."
Total unpaid leasing fees owed to joint ventures now total $600 million, the China Economic Times said.
By end-1996, a total of 36 Sino-foreign joint venture leasing firms had been set up in China, it said.

China Orient, once an active player in China's financial leasing sector, made net profits of $18 million. But payment delays began to appear from 1987, its problems have been growing worse and its business has slowed, the official said.
Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates also contributed to rising payment defaults, he said. Some firms insisted on paying at exchange rates favourable to them -- or not at all.
Others even resorted to fake bankruptcies to avoid repayment of their debts.
"We also have a certain amount of late payments on our books," an official of the Shanghai-based China International Leasing Company said by telephone.
The company was set up in 1985 by Mitsui & Company Ltd of Japan, the China National Technology Import and Export Corp and the China Investment Bank, he said.
The firm, the largest joint venture leasing company in China with total assets of $300 million, remained profitable in 1996 despite the unpaid fees, the official said.
"I believe the current problems are just short-term... I'm confident about the future," he said, but echoed the careful approach of China Orient.
"We are very cautious in selecting projects now," he said.
Leasing firms were now trying to find financial institutions and big firms to act as guarantors when signing new agreements.

The mounting problems of repayments prompted the government last July to allocate $200 million in loans to help state firms pay off their debts to leasing firms. Late last year, the State Economic and Trade Commission and the People's Bank of China, the central bank, ordered faster repayment to leasing firms.
